replacement: “And I never expected that!” cried Mitya, ecstatic. (He was still in a state of ecstasy.) He seized his six roubles and ran home. There he borrowed three roubles from the people of the house. They were so fond of him that they handed it over gladly, though it was all they had. In his excitement Mitya told them right then that his fate would be decided that day. In desperate haste he described the whole scheme he had put to Samsonov, how Samsonov had decided, what he himself hoped for the future, and so on. These people had been told many of their lodger’s secrets before, so they saw him as a gentleman with no pride at all, almost one of themselves. Now that he had nine roubles, Mitya sent for posting-horses to take him to the Volovya station. This is how it came to be remembered and put on record that “at midday, on the day before the event, Mitya had not a farthing, and that he had sold his watch to get money and had borrowed three roubles from his landlord, all in the presence of witnesses.”

First, he was late. He took a short cut from Volovya station, and it turned out to be eighteen versts instead of twelve. Second, the priest was not at home in Ilyinskoe. He had gone off to a neighboring village. As Mitya set out there with the same worn-out horses and looked for him, it was almost dark.
“No, you show me this: name me the law that allows roguery. D’you hear? You’re a scoundrel! Do you understand that?”
